column2: On the authority of Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with them both), from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, in what he relates from his Lord, Blessed and Exalted is He, who said: “Allah has written down the good deeds and the bad deeds, and then He made that clear.
Whoever intends a good deed but does not do it, Allah writes it down with Himself as a complete good deed;
and if he intends it and does it, Allah writes it down with Himself as ten good deeds, up to seven hundred times, up to many times more.
And if he intends a bad deed but does not do it, Allah writes it down with Himself as a complete good deed;
and if he intends it and does it, Allah writes it down as a single bad deed.” Reported by al-Bukhārī and Muslim.
Tabāraka (“Blessed is He”): far removed and holy; wa-taʿālā (“and Exalted”): above the attributes of creation, because of His perfection and loftiness.

Kataba (“has written down”): has decreed the measures of good and bad deeds. “Then He made that clear”: He set out in detail what He had stated in summary. “Whoever intends a good deed”: resolves to do it,
“but does not do it”: does not perform it,

“Allah writes it down”: Allah commands the recording angels to write it down. ʿIndahu (“with Himself”): as an honour. “A complete good deed”: with no deficiency in it. “And if he intends it and does it”: performs it, “Allah writes it down with Himself”: out of care for its doer and as an honour for him,
“as ten good deeds”: multiplied; and it may be multiplied many times over, according to the doer's intention, his sincerity and the benefits [of the deed].
“And if he intends a bad deed but does not do it”: leaves it out of fear of Allah, Allah, Glorified is He, writes it for him as a complete good deed.
“And if he does a bad deed, Allah writes it for him as a single one”: and He did not say “with Himself”, since no care is given to it or to its doer.
Using detail after summary, so that it makes a deeper impression and is more likely to be accepted.
The good and bad deeds a person does in this world have been written by Allah the Exalted in the Preserved Tablet.
It is part of Allah the Exalted's favour to His servants that whoever resolves to do a good deed and then leaves it, not doing it, has a complete good deed written for him.
Whoever resolves to do a good deed and does it, its reward is multiplied for him tenfold up to many times more.
It is part of Allah the Exalted's mercy to His servants that bad deeds are not multiplied; this does not prevent their becoming graver according to the deed.
Allah has honoured the doer of good deeds by writing his good deeds with Himself, indicating his nearness to Him.
Whoever does bad deeds and persists in them, without bringing good deeds to wipe them out, is far from Allah, Glorified is He.
Whoever intends a bad deed but does not do it, Allah writes it down with Himself as a complete good deed.

This ḥadīth qudsī contains great good news for the Muslims: whoever intends a good deed but does not do it, Allah writes it down with Himself as a complete good deed; and if he intends it and does it, Allah writes it for him with Himself as ten good deeds, up to many times more;

and if he intends a bad deed but does not do it, out of fear of Allah and His punishment, Allah writes it for him as a good deed for not venturing upon it; and if he does it, Allah the Exalted writes it as a single bad deed.

So look, my Muslim brother—may Allah grant you success in every good—at Allah's favour to His servants: Allah, Glorified is He, gives the one who does good deeds this great, multiplied favour, stressing, Glorified is He, that it is preserved with Him, to honour its doer;

while a bad deed, when it is done, He stressed is written as one only, describing it neither as complete nor as “with Himself”, since no care is given to it. So to Allah be praise for His blessings, which cannot be counted or numbered: “And if you should count the blessings of Allah, you could not enumerate them” [Ibrāhīm 14:34].
The stages of intention are five, they mentioned: a passing notion (hājis), / then a thought (khāṭir), then self-talk (ḥadīth al-nafs)—so listen;
after it comes inclination (hamm), then resolve (ʿazm). All are lifted / except the last, for which one is taken to account.
